reason: Shading tails of the normal curve shows why the conditional probability divides by the accepted region, and the sample-mean curve shows why the test uses a narrower distribution.

scenes.title: Premium fleeces inside the accepted fleeces
scenes.purpose: See that the premium region sits wholly inside the accepted region, so the numerator is just P(F>3) and the denominator is the accepted area.

steps.text: The blue-shaded region is the accepted fleeces, $F \geqslant 2$, with area $0.909$. Because you are told the fleece was accepted, this is the new whole: the denominator. This is the M1 for writing $\mathrm{P}(F>3 \mid F\geqslant 2)$ as a ratio.
The darker region, $F>3$, lies entirely inside the accepted region. So $\mathrm{P}(F>3 \cap F\geqslant 2)=\mathrm{P}(F>3)=0.187$, giving $\dfrac{0.187}{0.909}$. This is the A1ft.

Drag the threshold $k$ up to $2.6$ and the accepted area shrinks, so the ratio rises. At $k=2$ the answer is $\dfrac{0.18703}{0.90878}\approx 0.206$, the A1cso. Dividing by $\mathrm{P}(F>3)$ instead would be the common slip.

guide.what_you_see: The normal density curve for the fleece mass $F \sim \mathrm{N}(2.6, 0.45^2)$, with the accepted fleeces shaded from a movable threshold $k$ to the right and the premium fleeces ($F>3$) shaded more darkly inside that region.

legend.meaning: The density curve of $F$, the fleece mass in kg, with mean $2.6$ and standard deviation $0.45$. Areas under it are probabilities.
The lighter blue region under the curve from $x=k$ to the right-hand end. At $k=2$ it is the accepted fleeces, $\mathrm{P}(F\geqslant 2)$, the denominator of the conditional probability.
The darker region under the curve for $F>3$, the premium fleeces. It lies wholly inside $B$, so it is the numerator $\mathrm{P}(F>3)$.
The vertical line at $x=3$, the premium boundary of $3$ kg.
The dashed vertical line at $x=k$, the left-hand edge of the accepted region.

interact.do: Start at $k=2$, the acceptance threshold in the question, then drag the slider up towards $2.6$ and back down to $1$.
interact.watch: The dashed line moves and the accepted area shrinks as $k$ rises. At $k=2$ it reads about $0.909$, while the premium area stays at about $0.187$. So the ratio $\frac{0.187}{\text{accepted area}}$ rises above $0.206$ as $k$ increases, and only equals $0.206$ at $k=2$.

question_link.text: The blue region $B$ at $k=2$ is the accepted fleeces, so it is the new whole in $\mathrm{P}(F>3 \mid F\geqslant 2)$ (the M1). The darker region $A$ sits entirely inside it, so the numerator is just $\mathrm{P}(F>3)$, giving $\frac{0.187}{0.909}$ (the A1ft) and the value $0.206$ (the A1cso).

read_off: The live label 'Premium area P(F>3)' is the area of $A$, the probability $\mathrm{P}(F>3)\approx 0.187$ from part (b). It does not change when you move $k$.
The live label 'Accepted area' is the area of $B$, the probability that $F\geqslant k$. At $k=2$ it is about $0.909$, the value from part (a), and it is the denominator of your fraction.

scenes.title: Why the sample mean is tested on a narrower curve
scenes.purpose: See that the mean of 20 fleeces varies much less than one fleece, so 2.78 kg falls in the upper tail under the null hypothesis.

elements.value: Tail area for the sample mean = {area(T)}

steps.text: State $\mathrm{H_0}: \mu=2.6$ and $\mathrm{H_1}: \mu>2.6$. The dashed curve is a single fleece, with standard deviation $0.45$. The tall curve is the mean of 20 fleeces under $\mathrm{H_0}$, with standard deviation $\dfrac{0.45}{\sqrt{20}}\approx 0.1006$. This is the first M1.

With $m=2.78$, the shaded tail is $\mathrm{P}(\bar{F}\geqslant 2.78)\approx 0.0368$, which is less than $0.05$. This is the second M1. On the wide curve the tail would be about $0.345$, the scaling slip.

Drag $m$ below the dashed green line at the critical value $2.766$ and the tail area passes $0.05$, so you would not reject. At $2.78$ you reject $\mathrm{H_0}$: there is sufficient evidence that the mineral licks have increased the mean fleece mass. This is the A1.

guide.what_you_see: Two normal curves centred on the null-hypothesis mean $2.6$ kg: a wide dashed curve for one fleece and a tall narrow curve for the mean of 20 fleeces. The upper tail of the narrow curve is shaded from the slider value $m$ upwards.

legend.meaning: The distribution of the sample mean $\bar{F}$ of 20 fleeces under $\mathrm{H_0}$: $\mathrm{N}\left(2.6,\ \frac{0.45^2}{20}\right)$, with standard deviation $\frac{0.45}{\sqrt{20}}\approx 0.1006$.
The dashed curve for a single fleece, $F\sim\mathrm{N}(2.6,\ 0.45^2)$, with the larger standard deviation $0.45$. It shows what you get if you forget to scale.
The shaded upper tail of the sample-mean curve from $m$ to the right-hand edge, which is $\mathrm{P}(\bar{F}\geqslant m)$ under $\mathrm{H_0}$, the p-value when $m$ is the observed mean.
The vertical line at the slider value $m$, the sample mean being tested (start at $2.78$ kg).
The dashed green line at the critical value $2.766$ kg; a sample mean at or above it is in the rejection region at the 5% level.

interact.do: Start at $m=2.78$, then drag the slider left towards $2.4$ and right towards $3.2$, passing the green dashed line at $2.766$.
interact.watch: At $m=2.78$ the tail area reads about $0.0368$, below $0.05$, so you reject $\mathrm{H_0}$. As $m$ falls to $2.766$ the area rises to $0.05$, and below that it is larger than $0.05$, so you would not reject. Moving right makes the tail shrink towards $0$.

question_link.text: The tall curve $S$ is the distribution of $\bar{F}$ under $\mathrm{H_0}: \mu=2.6$ with standard deviation $\frac{0.45}{\sqrt{20}}$, which is the first M1. The shaded tail $T$ at $m=2.78$ is $\mathrm{P}(\bar{F}\geqslant 2.78)\approx 0.0368$, compared with $0.05$ for the second M1, and it supports the A1 conclusion, with $\mathrm{H_1}: \mu>2.6$, that the licks have raised the mean fleece mass.

read_off: The live label 'Tail area for the sample mean' is $\mathrm{P}(\bar{F}\geqslant m)$ under $\mathrm{H_0}$. At $m=2.78$ it is about $0.0368$, which you compare with the $0.05$ significance level; a value below $0.05$ means reject $\mathrm{H_0}$.
